hints: Think about what type of catalyst is needed to polarise $\text{Br}_2$ in the dark for ring bromination, recall the catalyst used for bromination of benzene.
walkthrough:
Spot the type of reaction**
You have methylbenzene plus bromine in the dark with a catalyst. That tells you this is electrophilic substitution on the ring, not free radical substitution on the side chain. For that you need a strong electrophile, $\text{Br}^+$.

See how the catalyst creates the electrophile**
$\text{Br}_2$ alone is not electrophilic enough. A Lewis acid such as $\text{AlBr}_3$ accepts a bromide ion from $\text{Br}_2$, leaving $\text{Br}^+$ and forming $\text{AlBr}_4^-$. So the completed equation is $\text{Br}_2 + \text{AlBr}_3 \rightarrow \text{Br}^+ + \text{AlBr}_4^-$.

hints: Draw the three possible ring substituted products of methylbenzene and label the positions relative to $\text{CH}_3$ as 2, 3 and 4.
Recall whether an alkyl group such as $\text{CH}_3$ directs an incoming electrophile to 2,4,6 positions or to 3,5 positions.
walkthrough:
Picture the three isomers**
Methylbenzene can be attacked at positions 2 and 6 (ortho), 3 and 5 (meta) and 4 (para) relative to $\text{CH}_3$. That gives 2-bromomethylbenzene, 3-bromomethylbenzene and 4-bromomethylbenzene.

Remember what methyl does**
A $\text{CH}_3$ group pushes electron density into the ring and activates the 2, 4 and 6 positions especially. In other words it is 2,4-directing, ortho and para directing. Attack at those positions gives a more stable intermediate.

Pick the odd one out**
The meta isomer, with $\text{Br}$ at position 3 relative to $\text{CH}_3$, does not benefit from this directing effect. So 3-bromomethylbenzene forms in much the smallest amount.

Final answer: Structure: 3-bromo-1-methylbenzene, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{Br}$ in meta positions on benzene ring.
$\text{CH}_3$ group is 2,4,6-directing (ortho and para directing), so substitution at the 3-position (meta) is disfavoured and forms least.

hints: Start from the pi electrons of the benzene ring attacking $\text{Br}^+$, show where the first curly arrow begins and ends.
Think about what the ring looks like after $\text{Br}$ has added but before $\text{H}^+$ is lost, charge and tetrahedral carbon.
Consider how aromaticity is restored by breaking the $\text{C-H}$ bond at the site of attack.
walkthrough:
Make the first bond to the electrophile**
Think of the benzene pi cloud as the nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the hexagon and pointing to the $\text{Br}^+$. That forms a new $\text{C-Br}$ bond at, for example, the 2-position next to $\text{CH}_3$.

Draw the Wheland intermediate correctly**
Once $\text{Br}$ adds, that carbon becomes tetrahedral and carries $\text{CH}_3$ nearby, plus the new $\text{Br}$ and the original $\text{H}$. The ring loses aromaticity and carries a positive charge delocalised over the remaining five carbons. Show the + in the ring and the $sp^3$ carbon clearly.

Restore the aromatic ring**
A base removes the $\text{H}^+$ from the same carbon that was attacked. Draw a curly arrow from that $\text{C-H}$ bond back into the hexagon to reform the pi system. The organic product is 2-bromomethylbenzene and the other product is $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from pi system inside hexagon to $\text{Br}^+$; arenium intermediate with $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{Br}$ and $\text{H}$ on $sp^3$ carbon and + charge delocalised in ring; curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond back into ring to reform aromatic system giving 2-bromomethylbenzene + $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Compare the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond in a saturated alkyl chloride with that in chlorobenzene and decide which $\text{Cl}$ can be released as $\text{Cl}^-$ by warm water.
walkthrough:
Link release of chloride to the precipitate**
Warm aqueous $\text{AgNO}_3$ only gives a precipitate if free $\text{Cl}^-$ is produced to meet $\text{Ag}^+$. A halogenoalkane like chlorobutane hydrolyses slowly in warm water to release $\text{Cl}^-$, so you see a white precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$. Chlorobenzene does not release $\text{Cl}^-$ under these conditions, so no precipitate.
Final answer: Chlorobutane reacts; white precipitate forms (chlorobenzene shows no reaction).

hints: Write first how $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$ reacts with water to form the alcohol and release chloride ions and hydrogen ions.
Write then what happens when the released chloride ion meets $\text{Ag}^+$ from silver nitrate.
walkthrough:
Show the slow hydrolysis step**
In warm water the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond in chlorobutane breaks by nucleophilic substitution by water: $$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Cl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH} + \text{H}^+ + \text{Cl}^-$$ This is the source of $\text{Cl}^-$. It is slow, which is why the precipitate appears slowly.

Show the precipitation step**
Once $\text{Cl}^-$ is free it instantly combines with $\text{Ag}^+$: $$\text{Ag}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{AgCl}$$ $\text{AgCl}$ is the white solid you observe.

hints: Look at the lone pairs on $\text{Cl}$ in chlorobenzene and how they can interact with the delocalised pi electrons of the ring.
Think about what this overlap does to the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond order and bond strength compared with a normal single $\text{C-Cl}$ bond.
walkthrough:
See the overlap in chlorobenzene**
In chlorobenzene the $\text{Cl}$ atom sits directly on the ring. One of its filled 3p lone pair orbitals can overlap sideways with the pi system of the ring. That means the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.

Connect delocalisation to bond strength**
Because of that overlap the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is no longer a pure single bond, it gains partial double bond character. It is shorter and stronger than the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond in chlorobutane. Much more energy is needed to break it, so warm aqueous $\text{AgNO}_3$ cannot hydrolyse chlorobenzene and no $\text{Cl}^-$ is released.

Final answer: Lone pair on $\text{Cl}$ is delocalised into the benzene pi system.
This gives the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond partial double bond character, strengthening it so it is not broken by warm water.
